blocks.text: Push a straight cutlass halfway into a bucket of water and it looks bent at the surface. Reach for a coin at the bottom of the same bucket and your fingers land short — the water is deeper than it looks. Light did not stop travelling in straight lines; it simply changed direction as it crossed from water into air.

blocks.markdown:
**Refraction** is the change in direction of light as it passes from one transparent medium into another. It happens because light travels at different speeds in different media. Light slows down on entering a denser medium and speeds up on leaving it.

The rule for which way it bends is worth learning as a sentence:

- Going from a **less dense to a denser** medium (air into glass), light slows down and bends **towards the normal**, so $r < i$.
- Going from a **denser to a less dense** medium (glass into air), light speeds up and bends **away from the normal**, so $r > i$.

A ray striking the surface **along the normal** ($i = 0$) passes straight through undeviated, though its speed still changes.

blocks.title: Snell's law
blocks.text: For light passing from one medium into another, the ratio of the sine of the angle of incidence to the sine of the angle of refraction is a constant. That constant is the refractive index of the second medium with respect to the first.

blocks.caption: Snell's law for light travelling from air into a medium of refractive index n

blocks.markdown:
Refractive index can be written in three equivalent ways, and WAEC uses all three:

$$n = \frac{\sin i}{\sin r} = \frac{\text{speed of light in vacuum}}{\text{speed of light in the medium}} = \frac{\text{real depth}}{\text{apparent depth}}$$

Refractive index has **no unit** — it is a ratio of two quantities of the same kind. Because light is always slower in a material than in a vacuum, $n$ for any real medium is always **greater than 1**.

blocks.caption: The denser the medium optically, the slower the light and the smaller the critical angle.

blocks.title: Using Snell's law
blocks.prompt: A ray of light travelling in air strikes the flat surface of a glass block at an angle of incidence of 30°. If the refractive index of the glass is 1.50, calculate the angle of refraction.

steps.text: Write Snell's law and make sin r the subject.
Check that the answer is sensible: the ray entered a denser medium, so r must be smaller than i, and 19.5° < 30°.

blocks.answer: The angle of refraction is about 19.5°

blocks.title: From refractive index to speed
blocks.prompt: The refractive index of glass is 1.50 and the speed of light in vacuum is 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s. Calculate the speed of light in the glass.

steps.text: Use the speed definition of refractive index.
State the answer with its unit.

blocks.answer: 2.0 × 10⁸ m/s, which is two-thirds of the speed in vacuum

blocks.markdown:
### Total internal reflection and the critical angle

When light travels from a **denser to a less dense** medium, the refracted ray bends away from the normal. Increase $i$ and the refracted ray swings further and further round until, at one particular angle of incidence, it just grazes along the boundary with $r = 90^\circ$. That angle of incidence is the **critical angle** $C$.

Increase $i$ beyond $C$ and no light escapes at all — the whole beam is reflected back into the denser medium, obeying the ordinary laws of reflection. This is **total internal reflection**.

blocks.caption: The critical angle for a medium of refractive index n bounded by air

blocks.title: The two conditions for total internal reflection
blocks.text: BOTH must hold: (1) the light must be travelling from an optically denser medium to an optically less dense one, and (2) the angle of incidence in the denser medium must be greater than the critical angle. Light going from air into glass can never be totally internally reflected, no matter what the angle.

blocks.title: Critical angle of glass
blocks.prompt: Calculate the critical angle for a glass–air boundary if the refractive index of the glass is 1.50.

steps.text: At the critical angle the refracted ray grazes the surface, r = 90°, which reduces Snell's law to a simple form.

blocks.answer: About 41.8°, so any ray inside the glass striking the surface at more than 41.8° is totally internally reflected

items: Mirages on a hot tarred road: hot air near the surface is less dense, so light from the sky is totally internally reflected upwards and the road looks wet.
Optical fibres for internet and endoscopes: light is trapped inside the fibre by repeated total internal reflection and follows it round bends.
Prism periscopes and binoculars: right-angled glass prisms turn light through 90° with almost no loss of brightness, better than a silvered mirror.
The sparkle of a well-cut diamond: its critical angle of only 24.4° means most light entering is reflected many times before it escapes.

blocks.markdown:
### Real and apparent depth

Rays from a coin at the bottom of a bucket bend away from the normal as they leave the water. To the eye above they seem to come from a point nearer the surface, so the water looks shallower than it is:

$$n = \frac{\text{real depth}}{\text{apparent depth}}$$

Because $n > 1$, the apparent depth is always **less** than the real depth. The vertical displacement of the image is $\text{real} - \text{apparent}$.

blocks.title: How shallow does the pond look?
blocks.prompt: A pond is 1.2 m deep. If the refractive index of water is 4/3, calculate the apparent depth of the pond when viewed from directly above.

steps.text: Substitute the real depth and n = 4/3.
State the answer with its unit.
The bottom therefore appears raised by 1.2 − 0.90 = 0.30 m, which is why non-swimmers misjudge water depth.

blocks.answer: 0.90 m, an apparent rise of 0.30 m

blocks.title: Common errors
blocks.text: Do not use sin i / sin r with i measured from the surface — always from the normal. When light goes from glass into air, the index to use is 1/n, not n, so sin i / sin r = 1/1.5 for a glass-to-air ray. And divide by n to get apparent depth, never multiply, or you will make the pond deeper than it really is.

blocks.title: WAEC and JAMB tip
blocks.text: Set your calculator to degrees before working with sines. If an answer for r comes out bigger than i when the ray entered a denser medium, you have inverted the formula — check before you write it down.

points: Refraction is the bending of light at a boundary, caused by a change in the speed of light between the two media.
Light bends towards the normal entering a denser medium and away from the normal leaving it; a ray along the normal is undeviated.
Snell's law: n = sin i / sin r, and equivalently n = c/v = real depth / apparent depth. Refractive index has no unit and is greater than 1.
The critical angle satisfies sin C = 1/n, so a denser medium has a smaller critical angle.
Total internal reflection needs light going from denser to less dense AND an angle of incidence greater than C; it explains mirages, optical fibres and prism periscopes.
Apparent depth = real depth ÷ n, so water always looks shallower than it is.
